lead: The orange juice or vitamin C diet is a practice of drinking large amounts of citrus juice, or taking high amounts of vitamin C, with the aim of a brighter, healthier-looking complexion. The reasoning is that vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that build stable collagen, the protein that gives skin firmness, so people who want firmer, glowing skin try to keep their intake high.[2]

Orange juice is a convenient source: a 250 mL cup provides a large share of daily vitamin C along with about 21 g of sugar.[1] Some community members treat juice as an add-on to protein-heavy or low-carbohydrate eating, while others discuss it as mostly sugar with some vitamin C.[3]

Reference sources describe the US recommended intake as 90 mg/day for men and 75 mg/day for women, and note that absorption efficiency falls at large doses and excess is excreted in urine.[2] No published trial has tested orange-juice-centred protocols for skin appearance.

chain: Higher vitamin C intake from juice or supplements
More vitamin C available for collagen-building enzymes
angle.text: Followers drink orange juice or raise vitamin C intake hoping for firmer, brighter skin, since vitamin C is needed for collagen formation. Orange juice also adds fluid and a small amount of citrus flavonoids to the diet.

paras: A 250 mL cup of orange juice has about 112 calories and 21 g of sugar and is a rich source of vitamin C.[1] Oranges and lemons contain roughly 53 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, and pasteurisation and cooking reduce the content of foods.[2]

Vitamin C is needed for enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, and prolonged deficiency causes scurvy.[2] Active transport absorbs most vitamin C at ordinary intakes, absorption efficiency falls at large doses, and plasma levels saturate at modest intakes.[2]
Orange juice also contains flavonoids, and reviews have discussed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of orange juice in general.[4]

On looksmax.org, orange juice appears in diet threads where members weigh its vitamin C against its sugar and carbohydrate content, and in light-hearted questions about whether drinking it counts as improving looks.[3]

No studies found on orange-juice-centred diets for skin appearance. Trials of orange juice in other settings include a randomized trial of flavonoid-rich orange juice in young adults with depression and a trial of daily orange consumption in fatty liver disease, which did not look at skin.[5][6]

The US Institute of Medicine set a 2,000 mg/day upper level in 2000 based on gastrointestinal effects seen above 3,000 mg/day, while the European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence to set one.[2] Orange juice is acidic and sugar-rich, and some government guidance favours whole fruit over juice.[1]

lore.intro: Online, citrus and vitamin C are discussed for brighter skin, with members debating juice against whole foods and supplements.[3]

claims.claim: High vitamin C or orange juice intake improves skin quality
claims.believers: Proponents cite vitamin C's role in collagen synthesis.[2]
claims.experts: Reference works describe vitamin C's collagen role and note that absorption saturates; no studies of juice-based protocols for skin were found.[2]

claims.claim: Orange juice is mostly sugar with little nutritional value
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread participant describes juice as largely sugar with a low amount of vitamin C.[3]
claims.experts: Reference sources list a cup as about 21 g of sugar and a rich vitamin C source, and describe its health value as debated.[1]

name: Orange juice / vitamin C diet

card.summary: Heavy orange juice or vitamin C intake for skin, resting on vitamin C's collagen role; untested for appearance and sugar-heavy.
card.note: High doses cause GI effects; juice is high in sugar.

quick.overview:
This practice involves taking in large amounts of orange juice or vitamin C for skin. The idea rests on vitamin C's role in collagen formation.

No studies have tested it for appearance, and orange juice is high in sugar.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin C is a cofactor for collagen-building enzymes; whether extra intake beyond adequacy changes skin is untested in this context.
quick.risks: Doses above about 3,000 mg/day have caused diarrhea and other gastrointestinal effects, and the US upper level is 2,000 mg/day.
